blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — look-alike medication packaging
stem: A nurse notices that two different medications have very similar container labels and packaging. No error has occurred yet. What is the best action?

options.A: Report the look-alike packaging through the medication-safety process so the hazard can be evaluated before it contributes to a wrong-drug error.
options.B: Continue routine use without reporting the similarity because a packaging concern becomes a medication-safety issue only after patient harm occurs.
options.C: Rely on staff familiarity with the products and reinforce memorization of label differences instead of escalating the packaging concern.
options.D: Assume the packaging is adequately differentiated because both medications have FDA-approved labeling and are stocked in the same facility.

rationale: A is correct. FDA identifies look-alike container labels as a preventable medication-error hazard and encourages healthcare providers to report medication errors as well as circumstances such as similar packaging or labeling that may cause or lead to an error. B waits for harm unnecessarily. C relies on memory rather than hazard reporting and system mitigation. D incorrectly assumes FDA approval means the products cannot present a look-alike medication-error risk.
educational_objective: Recognize and report look-alike drug labeling or packaging as a preventable medication-safety hazard before an error occurs.
source_organization: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA); NCSBN
source_document_title: Medication Errors Related to CDER-Regulated Drug Products; Instructions for Completing Form FDA 3500; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: Current FDA medication-error pages live-rechecked 2026-08-21; FDA container-label guidance final May 2022; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective April 2026
source_locator: FDA Medication Errors page: wrong drug due to look-alike container labels is a preventable event; FDA encourages reporting medication errors and circumstances such as look-alike container labels that may cause or lead to an error. FDA Form 3500 instructions: report circumstances/events with capacity to cause error, including similar product appearance, packaging/labeling, and look-alike names.
source_claim_supported: Current FDA guidance directly supports recognizing look-alike packaging as a preventable medication-error hazard and reporting hazardous circumstances before patient harm occurs.
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — medication-error prevention, hazard recognition, and appropriate safety reporting.
pdf_visual_verification: PASS — relevant official 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan safety content was screenshot-verified earlier in this continuation; medication-error claims rely on current FDA HTML.

option_audit.A: Correct; directly applies FDA's proactive reporting approach to a look-alike packaging hazard.
option_audit.B: Plausible event-trigger misconception but FDA explicitly includes circumstances that may cause an error even before harm.
option_audit.C: Plausible education-only response but does not address the system-level packaging hazard.
option_audit.D: Plausible regulatory-assurance misconception but approved products can still generate postmarketing medication-error risks.

cueing_audit.answer_length: All options are similar in professional tone and detail; the key is not uniquely signaled by length.
cueing_audit.absolute_words: No distractor depends on simplistic always/never/only wording.
